{{short description|American physicist}}
'''Robert W. Bussard''' (August 11, 1928 &ndash; October 6, 2007) was an American [[physicist]] who worked primarily in [[nuclear fusion]] energy research. He was the recipient of the Schreiber–Spence Space Achievement Award for STAIF-2004.<ref>[http://www.unm.edu/~isnps/staifarchives/staif2004.html STAIF-2004 Archives] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070128131513/http://www.unm.edu/~isnps/staifarchives/staif2004.html |date=January 28, 2007 }}</ref> He was also a fellow of the [[International Academy of Astronautics]] and held a Ph.D. from [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Robert W Bussard {{!}} The Space Show |url=https://www.thespaceshow.com/guest/dr.-robert-w-bussard-0 |access-date=2023-01-21 |website=www.thespaceshow.com}}</ref>

== Kiwi (Rover-A) ==
In June 1955 Bussard moved to Los Alamos and joined the Nuclear Propulsion Division's [[Project Rover]] designing  [[nuclear thermal rocket]] engines.<ref name="bussard">Bussard, Robert.  "Nuclear Rocketry - The First Bright Hopes", Astronautics, Vol. 7, No. 12, Dec. 1962, pp. 32–35</ref> Bussard and R.D. DeLauer wrote two important monographs on nuclear propulsion, ''Nuclear Rocket Propulsion''<ref name="Nuc Prop">{{Cite book |last=Bussard |first=R. W. |last2=DeLauer |first2=R.D. |year=1958 |title=Nuclear Rocket Propulsion |publisher=McGraw-Hill}}</ref> and ''Fundamentals of Nuclear Flight''.<ref name="Nuc Flight">{{Cite book |last=Bussard |first=R.W. |last2=DeLauer |first2=R. D. |year=1965 |title=Fundamentals of Nuclear Flight |publisher=McGraw-Hill}}</ref>

== Bussard ramjet ==
In 1960, Bussard<ref>Bussard, R.W., “Galactic Matter and Interstellar Flight”, Acta Astronatica, VI, pp. 179–195, 1960.</ref> conceived of the [[Bussard ramjet]], an interstellar [[outer space|space]] drive powered by [[hydrogen]] fusion using hydrogen collected with a [[magnetic field]] from the interstellar gas. Due to the presence of high-energy particles throughout space, much of the [[Interstellar medium|interstellar hydrogen]] exists in an [[ion]]ized state (H II regions) that can be manipulated by [[magnetic field|magnetic]] or [[electric field]]s. Bussard proposed to "scoop" up ionized hydrogen and funnel it into a fusion reactor, using the exhaust from the reactor as a rocket engine.<ref>R.W.Bussard, "Fusion as Electric Propulsion", "Journal of Propulsion and Power" v6 no September 5–October 1990, pp. 567–574</ref>

It appears the energy gain in the reactor must be extremely high for the ramjet to work at all; any hydrogen picked up by the scoop must be sped up to the same speed as the ship in order to provide thrust, and the energy required to do so increases with the ship's speed. [[Proton–proton chain|Hydrogen itself]] does not fuse very well (unlike deuterium, which is rare in the interstellar medium), and so cannot be used directly to produce energy, a fact which accounts for the billion-year scale of stellar lifetimes. This problem was solved, in principle, according to Bussard, by use of the stellar [[CNO cycle]], in which carbon is used as a catalyst to burn hydrogen via the strong nuclear reaction.<ref>Whitmire, D. "Relativistic spaceflight and the catalytic nuclear ramjet", Acta Astronautica, 2, 497–509, 1975.</ref>

=== In science fiction ===
Bussard Ramjets are common plot devices in science fiction.

[[Larry Niven]] uses them in his [[Known Space]] setting to propel interstellar flight.  Following a standard hi-tech faster/cheaper/better learning curve, he started with robot probes during the early stages of interstellar colonization and eventually plotted them as affordable to wealthy individuals relocating their families off a too-crowded Earth (in "The Ethics of Madness").  Niven also employed Bussard ramjets as the propulsion and stabilizing engines of the [[Ringworld]] (four novels), which were also set in Known Space.

In the ''[[Star Trek]]'' universe, a variation called the ''Bussard Hydrogen Collector'' or ''Bussard Ramscoop'' appears as part of the [[deuterium|matter]]–[[antimatter]] propulsion system that allows [[Starfleet]] ships to travel [[Faster-than-light|faster than the speed of light]]. The ramscoops attach to the front of the ''warp nacelles'', and when the ship's internal supply of deuterium runs low, they collect interstellar hydrogen and convert it to deuterium and anti-deuterium for use as the primary fuel in a starship's ''[[Warp drive (Star Trek)|warp drive]]''.

== Atomic Energy Commission ==
In the early 1970s Bussard became Assistant Director under Director [[Robert L. Hirsch|Robert Hirsch]] at the Controlled Thermonuclear Reaction Division of what was then known as the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]]. They founded the mainline fusion program for the United States based on the [[tokamak]]. Bussard left the AEC in 1973, after the funding of the [[Symmetrical Tokamak]] and [[Princeton Large Torus]] at [[PPPL]].

In June 1995, Bussard claimed in a letter to all fusion laboratories, as well as to key members of the US Congress, that he and the other founders of the program supported the tokamak not out of conviction that it was the best technical approach but rather as a vehicle for generating political support, thereby allowing them to pursue "all the hopeful new things the mainline labs would not try".<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.askmar.com/Robert%20Bussard/1995-6-6%20Letter%20to%20Congress.pdf |title=Bussard's Letter |access-date=March 12, 2010 |archive-date=July 2, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100702205827/http://www.askmar.com/Robert%20Bussard/1995-6-6%20Letter%20to%20Congress.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Independent fusion ventures ==

=== [[Riggatron]] and INESCO ===

In 1977 he founded the private company INESCO, International Nuclear Energy Systems Company, with [[Bruno Coppi]] to promote the [[riggatron]] nuclear fusion concept. It was among the earliest private fusion companies.<ref name="sdr">{{cite web|url=https://www.sandiegoreader.com/news/1983/feb/24/cover-the-man-who-would-make-stars/|title=General Atomics' local competitor in the race for fusion|date=1983-02-24|author=Jeannette DeWyze|work=San Diego Reader}}</ref> It did not ultimately get enough funding to build a riggatron.

=== Polywell fusor ===
{{Main|Polywell}}
Bussard worked on a promising new type of [[inertial electrostatic confinement]] (IEC) fusor, the [[polywell]], that has a magnetically shielded grid (MaGrid). He founded Energy/Matter Conversion Corporation, Inc. (EMC2) in 1985 to validate his theory,<ref name="firstpatent">{{ cite patent | country=US | number=4826646 | status=patent | title=Method and apparatus for controlling charged particles | gdate=1989-05-02 | fdate=1985-10-29 | pridate=1985-10-29 | inventor=Bussard, Robert W. | assign1=Energy/Matter Conversion Corporation, Inc.}}</ref> and tested several (15) experimental devices from 1994 through 2006. The U.S. Navy contract funding that supported the work expired while experiments were still small. However, the final tests of the last device, WB-6, reputedly solved the last remaining physics problem just as the funding expired and the EMC2 labs had to be shut down.

Further funding was eventually found, the work continued and the WB-7 prototype was constructed and tested, and the research is ongoing.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.askmar.com/ConferenceNotes/Should%20Google%20Go%20Nuclear.pdf |title=Should Google Go Nuclear? |access-date=October 21, 2010 |archive-date=June 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160604105239/http://www.askmar.com/ConferenceNotes/Should%20Google%20Go%20Nuclear.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Funding Polywell ===
During 2006 and 2007, Bussard sought the large-scale funding necessary to design and construct a full-scale Polywell fusion power plant.<ref name="google">{{Cite web |last=Dr. Robert Bussard (lecturer) |date=November 9, 2006 |title=''Should Google Go Nuclear? Clean, cheap, nuclear power (no, really)'' |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rk6z1vP4Eo8  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211212/rk6z1vP4Eo8| archive-date=2021-12-12 |url-status=live|access-date=July 15, 2014 |website=Google Tech Talks}}{{cbignore}}</ref> His fusor design is feasible enough, he asserted, to render unnecessary the construction of larger and larger test models still too small to achieve [[Fusion energy gain factor|break-even]]. Also, the scaling of power with size goes as the seventh power of the machine radius, while the gain scales as the fifth power, so there is little incentive to build half-scale systems; one might as well build the real thing.

On March 29, 2006, Bussard claimed on the fusor.net [[internet forum]] that EMC² had developed an [[inertial electrostatic confinement]] fusion process that was 100,000 times more efficient than previous designs, but that the US Navy budget line item that supported the work was zero-funded in FY2006.<ref name="fusor.net">{{Cite web |last=Robert W. Bussard |date=March 29, 2006 |title=''Inertial Electrostatic Fusion systems can now be built'' |url=http://www.fusor.net/board/view.php?site=fusor&bn=fusor_announce&key=1143684406 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070224220614/http://www.fusor.net/board/view.php?site=fusor&bn=fusor_announce&key=1143684406 |archive-date=February 24, 2007 |access-date=February 22, 2007 |website=fusor.net forums}}</ref>

Bussard provided more details of his breakthrough and the circumstances surrounding the end of his Navy funding in a letter to the ''James Randi Educational Foundation'' internet forum on June 23.<ref name="randi">{{Cite web |last=SirPhilip (posting an e-mail from "RW Bussard") |date=June 23, 2006 |title=''Fusion, eh?'' |url=http://forums.randi.org/showthread.php?t=58665#27 |access-date=February 22, 2007 |website=[[James Randi Educational Foundation]] forums |archive-date=September 29, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929091321/http://forums.randi.org/showthread.php?t=58665#27 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

From October 2, 2006, to October 6, 2006, Bussard presented an informal overview of the previous decade of his work at the 57th [[International Astronautical Congress]].<ref>[http://www.askmar.com/ConferenceNotes/2006-9%20IAC%20Paper.pdf ''The Advent of Clean Nuclear Fusion: Super-performance Space Power and Propulsion''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110929075949/http://www.askmar.com/ConferenceNotes/2006-9%20IAC%20Paper.pdf |date=September 29, 2011 }}, Robert W. Bussard, Ph.D., 57th International Astronautical Congress, October 2–6, 2006.</ref> This was the first publication of this work in 11&nbsp;years, as the U.S. Navy had put an embargo on publications of the research, in 1994.

Bussard presented further details of his IEC fusion research at a Google Tech Talk on November 9, 2006, of which a video was widely circulated.<ref name="google" />

Bussard presented more of his thoughts on the potential world impact of fusion power at a [[Yahoo!]] Tech Talk on April 10, 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.askmar.com/Fusion.html |title=''Askmar summary of IEC fusion'' |access-date=May 11, 2007 |archive-date=July 23, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080723182449/http://www.askmar.com/Fusion.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>
(The video is only available internally for Yahoo employees.) He also spoke on the internet talk radio show ''The Space Show'', Broadcast 709, on May 7, 2007.<ref name="space show">{{Cite episode |series=The Space Show |number=709 |credits=Hosted by Dr. David Livingston |airdate=May 7, 2007}}</ref>

He founded a non-profit organization to solicit tax-deductible donations to restart the work in 2007, EMC2 Fusion Development Corporation.<ref>{{Cite web|title=EMC2 Fusion Development Corporation|url=http://emc2fusion.org/|access-date=April 28, 2021|website=emc2fusion.org|archive-date=April 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430014529/http://www.emc2fusion.org/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Spaceflight===

In a 1998 [[Analog magazine]] article, fellow fusion researcher [[Tom Ligon]] described an easily  built demonstration fusor system along with some of Bussard's ideas for fusion reactors and incredibly powerful [[spacecraft propulsion]] systems, with which spacecraft could swiftly move throughout the solar system.<ref name="Analog Magazine">{{Cite journal |last=Ligon |first=Tom |date=December 12, 1998 |title=''The World's Simplest Fusion Reactor And How To Make It Work'' |journal=Analog Magazine}}</ref>

== Quotes ==
"Thus, we have the ability to do away with oil (and other fossil fuels) but it will take 4–6 years and [[wikt:circa|ca.]] $100–200M to build the full-scale plant and demonstrate it."<ref name="fusor.net" />

"Somebody will build it; and when it's built, it will work; and when it works people will begin to use it, and it will begin to displace all other forms of energy."<ref name="space show" />

== Death ==
Bussard died from [[multiple myeloma]] on October 6, 2007, at age 79.<ref>{{Cite web |last=M. Simon |date=October 8, 2007 |title=''Dr. Robert W. Bussard Has Passed'' |url=http://www.classicalvalues.com/archives/2007/10/dr_robert_w_bus.html |access-date=October 9, 2007 |website=Classical Values}}</ref>
